claim: Drosophila indirect flight muscles (IFMs) are formed during pupal development from a pool of undifferentiated myoblasts called adult muscle precursors (AMPs).
source: Like all Drosophila adult muscles, IFMs are formed during pupal development from a pool of undifferentiated myoblasts called adult muscle precursors (AMPs) (Bate et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bate et al., 1991

claim: From 8 hr after puparium formation (APF), AMPs either fuse with themselves (for the dorso-ventral flight muscles, DVMs) or with remodelled larval template muscles (for the dorso-longitudinal flight muscles, DLMs) to form myotubes.
source: From 8 hr after puparium formation (APF), these AMPs either fuse with themselves (for the dorso-ventral flight muscles, DVMs) or with remodelled larval template muscles (for the dorso-longitudinal flight muscles, DLMs) to form myotubes (Dutta et al., 2004; Fernandes et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dutta et al., 2004 and Fernandes et al., 1991

claim: Myotubes develop dynamic leading edges at both ends and initiate attachment to their respective tendon cells at 12 to 16 hr APF.
source: These myotubes develop dynamic leading edges at both ends and initiate attachment to their respective tendon cells at 12 to 16 hr APF (Weitkunat et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weitkunat et al., 2014

claim: The first immature periodic myofibrils form at 30 hr APF when the muscle fibers are about 150 µm in length.
source: These attachments mature and mechanical tension is built up in the myotubes, followed by the formation of the first immature periodic myofibrils at 30 hr APF when the muscle fibers are about 150 µm in length.
evidence: Stated directly in the text

claim: The earliest sarcomeres are about 1.8 µm in length.
source: These immature myofibrils contain the earliest sarcomeres, which are about 1.8 µm in length (Weitkunat et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weitkunat et al., 2014

claim: During the remaining 3 days of pupal development, the muscle fibers grow to about 1 mm to fill the entire thorax.
source: During the remaining 3 days of pupal development, the muscle fibers grow to about 1 mm to fill the entire thorax and sarcomere length increases to a final length of about 3.2 µm in adult flies (Orfanos et al., 2015; Reedy and Beall, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Orfanos et al., 2015 and Reedy and Beall, 1993

claim: Sarcomere length increases to a final length of about 3.2 µm in adult flies.
source: During the remaining 3 days of pupal development, the muscle fibers grow to about 1 mm to fill the entire thorax and sarcomere length increases to a final length of about 3.2 µm in adult flies (Orfanos et al., 2015; Reedy and Beall, 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Orfanos et al., 2015 and Reedy and Beall, 1993

claim: The flight muscle specific selector gene spalt major (spalt, salm) is turned on in the developing flight muscle myotubes after myoblasts have fused to myotubes.
source: After myoblasts have fused to myotubes, the flight muscle specific selector gene spalt major (spalt, salm) is turned on in the developing flight muscle myotubes.
evidence: Stated directly in the text

claim: Spalt major is responsible for the correct fate determination and development of the flight muscles, which includes the fibrillar flight muscle morphology and the stretch-activated muscle contraction mode.
source: Spalt major is responsible for the correct fate determination and development of the flight muscles, which includes the fibrillar flight muscle morphology and the stretch-activated muscle contraction mode (Schönbauer et al., 2011; Syme and Josephson, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schönbauer et al., 2011 and Syme and Josephson, 2002

claim: Spalt major controls the expression of more than 700 flight muscle specific genes or gene isoforms during development.
source: It does so by controlling the expression of more than 700 flight muscle specific genes or gene isoforms during development (Spletter and Schnorrer, 2014; Spletter et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Spletter and Schnorrer, 2014 and Spletter et al., 2015

claim: mRNA-Seq was performed using at least two biological replicates for each time point.
source: We performed mRNA-Seq using at least two biological replicates for each time point (see Materials and methods).

claim: Each of the 40 clusters contains a unique gene set ranging from 155 to 703 members.

claim: The major variance in the PCA of the mRNA-Seq time points and Mfuzz clusters is developmental time, with a notable change after 30 hr APF.

claim: Many sarcomeric genes are strongly up-regulated from 30 hr to 72 hr APF.

claim: Many genes are turned on from 30 hr to 72 hr APF, whereas others are already expressed at 30 hr and strongly increase their expression until 72 hr.
source: We noted that many genes are turned on from 30 hr to 72 hr APF, whereas others are already expressed at 30 hr and strongly increase their expression until 72 hr (Figure 4D), suggesting a transcriptional transition after 30 hr APF.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4D

claim: GO-terms of cell proliferation, cell cycle and Notch signalling are down-regulated from 30 hr to 72 hr APF.
source: Consistently, we found GO-terms of cell proliferation, cell cycle and Notch signalling down-regulated, whereas actin cytoskeleton, sarcomere, muscle function and mitochondrial related gene sets are strongly up-regulated from 30 hr to 72 hr APF (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Actin cytoskeleton, sarcomere, muscle function and mitochondrial related gene sets are strongly up-regulated from 30 hr to 72 hr APF.
source: Consistently, we found GO-terms of cell proliferation, cell cycle and Notch signalling down-regulated, whereas actin cytoskeleton, sarcomere, muscle function and mitochondrial related gene sets are strongly up-regulated from 30 hr to 72 hr APF (Figure 4E).

claim: The identified sarcomeric clusters 13 and 22 are enriched for 'salm-core genes'.
source: As the identified sarcomeric clusters 13 and 22 are enriched for 'salm-core genes' (Spletter et al., 2015) (Figure 3), we chose to investigate gene expression in developing spalt-major knock-down (salmIR) flight muscles compared to wild type (Supplementary file 4).

claim: Members of cluster 22 are not only down-regulated at 72 hr APF in salmIR but are also less strongly induced from 30 hr to 72 hr APF in salmIR muscle compared to wild type.
source: Interestingly, members of cluster 22, which is strongly enriched for sarcomeric and mitochondrial genes, are not only down-regulated at 72 hr APF in salmIR (Figure 6B) but are also less strongly induced from 30 hr to 72 hr APF in salmIR muscle compared to wild type (Figure 6D), suggesting that salm in addition to other factors is indeed required for the strong induction of sarcomeric protein expression after 30 hr APF.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6D

claim: Salm in addition to other factors is required for the strong induction of sarcomeric protein expression after 30 hr APF.
source: Interestingly, members of cluster 22, which is strongly enriched for sarcomeric and mitochondrial genes, are not only down-regulated at 72 hr APF in salmIR (Figure 6B) but are also less strongly induced from 30 hr to 72 hr APF in salmIR muscle compared to wild type (Figure 6D), suggesting that salm in addition to other factors is indeed required for the strong induction of sarcomeric protein expression after 30 hr APF.

claim: Act88F-GAL4 is expressed from about 18 hr APF and requires salm activity for its expression.

evidence: Supported by citations to Sevdali et al., 2013 and Wallgren-Pettersson et al., 2011

evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7J and Supplemental File 3

claim: Salm in addition to other factors is required for normal sarcomere maturation.
source: However, the sarcomeres of Act88F >> salmIR muscles displayed a strong defect in sarcomere length growth after 48 hr APF (Figure 7J, Supplemental File 3), with sarcomeres only obtaining a length of 2.8 µm in adult flies, demonstrating that Salm in addition to other factors is required for normal sarcomere maturation.

claim: Act88F >> salmIR flies are flightless.
source: As expected, Act88F >> salmIR flies are flightless (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and we observed rupturing of the adult muscle fibers within 1d after eclosion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–G), demonstrating the importance of proper sarcomere maturation to prevent muscle atrophy.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: Rupturing of the adult muscle fibers occurs within 1d after eclosion in Act88F >> salmIR flies.
source: As expected, Act88F >> salmIR flies are flightless (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and we observed rupturing of the adult muscle fibers within 1d after eclosion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–G), demonstrating the importance of proper sarcomere maturation to prevent muscle atrophy.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-G

claim: Proper sarcomere maturation is important to prevent muscle atrophy.
source: As expected, Act88F >> salmIR flies are flightless (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and we observed rupturing of the adult muscle fibers within 1d after eclosion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–G), demonstrating the importance of proper sarcomere maturation to prevent muscle atrophy.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that defective sarcomere maturation leads to muscle fiber rupturing

claim: At 48 hr APF, Act88F >> salmIR fibers twitch, but less often than and without the double twitches observed in control fibers.
source: At 48 hr APF, Act88F >> salmIR fibers twitch, but less often than and without the double twitches observed in control fibers (Figure 7K,L,O; Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7K,L,O and Figure 7—video 1

claim: At 72 hr APF salmIR fibers fail to stop contracting and show frequent and uncoordinated spontaneous contractions in which different myofibril bundles of the same fiber twitch at different times.
source: Strikingly, at 72 hr APF salmIR fibers fail to stop contracting and moreover show frequent and uncoordinated spontaneous contractions in which different myofibril bundles of the same fiber twitch at different times (Figure 7M–O, Figure 7—video 2), demonstrating that sarcomere maturation is indeed disrupted, with the likely consequence that myofibrils fail to acquire normal stretch-activation sensitivity.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7M-O and Figure 7—video 2

claim: Sarcomere maturation is disrupted in salmIR fibers, with the likely consequence that myofibrils fail to acquire normal stretch-activation sensitivity.
source: Strikingly, at 72 hr APF salmIR fibers fail to stop contracting and moreover show frequent and uncoordinated spontaneous contractions in which different myofibril bundles of the same fiber twitch at different times (Figure 7M–O, Figure 7—video 2), demonstrating that sarcomere maturation is indeed disrupted, with the likely consequence that myofibrils fail to acquire normal stretch-activation sensitivity.

claim: Sarcomeres are built of three filament types arrayed in a pseudo-crystalline order: actin filaments, muscle myosin filaments, and connecting filaments formed of titin molecules.
source: They are built of three filament types arrayed in a pseudo-crystalline order: actin filaments are cross-linked with their plus ends at the sarcomeric Z-disc and face with their minus ends towards the sarcomere center. In the center, symmetric bipolar muscle myosin filaments, anchored at the M-line, can interact with the actin filaments. Myosin movement towards the actin plus ends thus produces force during sarcomere shortening. Both filament types are permanently linked by a third filament type, the connecting filaments, formed of titin molecules (Gautel and Djinović-Carugo, 2016; Lange et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gautel and Djinović-Carugo, 2016 and Lange et al., 2006

claim: Sarcomeres have a stereotyped size, ranging from 3.0 to 3.4 µm in relaxed human skeletal muscle fibers.

evidence: Supported by citations to Ehler and Gautel, 2008; Llewellyn et al., 2008; and Regev et al., 2011

claim: The length of each bipolar myosin filament is 1.6 µm in all mature sarcomeres of vertebrate muscles, requiring about 300 myosin hexamers to assemble per filament.
